description: We are a passionate team exploring space technology, AI/ML, satellite data, Earth observation, and innovative problem-solving using NASA data and technology. We welcome members skilled in AI/ML, coding, web development, GIS, research, design, and communication to collaborate, learn, and build an impactful solution together!
summary:
**Summary (about 150 words)**

EarthDial is a conversational vision-language model for Earth observation. It turns satellite imagery into interactive, natural-language dialogue. It is fine-tuned from InternVL2, with a high-resolution visual encoder, an MLP projector and a Phi-3 Mini language model. It was trained in three stages on 11.11M instruction pairs covering RGB, SAR and multispectral data (including NIR and infrared), plus bi-temporal and multi-temporal sequences. It handles classification, detection, captioning, visual question answering, visual grounding and change detection in one assistant. A Streamlit demo lets users upload imagery and chat with the model.

It addresses a gap: generic vision-language models perform poorly on remote sensing data, and existing geo-spatial models are limited to a fixed resolution and a few sensor types. EarthDial supports many sensors, resolutions and time steps. The authors report it outperforms existing models on 44 benchmarks.

This matters because manual analysis can't keep up with the volume of Earth observation data. Plain-language access helps disaster response, environmental monitoring and resource management.

This summary is based on the project's README. If you're submitting it as your own work, adjust the wording to say what you personally contributed, such as the demo, the presentation or the video.
details:
Project details: EarthDial (based on the project's README, since I didn't run the model)

What it does and how it works. EarthDial is a chat assistant for satellite and aerial imagery. You give it an image and a question, and it answers in plain language. It can classify scenes, detect and ground objects, caption images or regions, answer visual questions, and compare images over time for change detection. Under the hood, a visual encoder reads the image at high resolution, an MLP projector converts the visual features into the language model's space, and a Phi-3 Mini language model (4B parameters) writes the answer. Task tokens and region inputs tell it what to do, and answers can include object locations. A Streamlit web demo lets users upload imagery and chat.

Benefits. One model covers many sensors (RGB, SAR, multispectral, NIR, infrared), resolutions and time steps, where earlier models were tied to one resolution or a few sensors. The authors report it outperforms generic and domain-specific models on 44 benchmarks. Users get answers in natural language and don't need remote sensing expertise.

Intended impact. Faster analysis of Earth observation data for disaster response, environmental monitoring and resource management. Weights and data are public on Hugging Face, so others can build on them.

Tools and hardware.

  • Python 3.9 and conda, with Hugging Face Transformers and Hugging Face Hub
  • Fine-tuned from InternVL2, with Phi-3 Mini as the language model
  • flash-attn for training
  • Streamlit for the demo, plus Docker
  • Training on 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, with batch size 128 and a learning rate of 4e-5
  • For my own part (the PPT and video): pptxgenjs, Pillow and FFmpeg

Creativity. It is the first remote-sensing vision-language model with grounding, according to the README. It also uses a data-generation pipeline that turns existing detection datasets into short descriptions and conversations, which produced 11.11M instruction pairs.

Factors considered.

  • Forgetting: three-stage training (conversational pretraining, then RGB and temporal, then multispectral and SAR) avoids losing earlier skills.
  • Reproducibility: evaluation uses greedy decoding, so results are consistent with the real-time chat demo.
  • Hardware: the README explains how to train on fewer GPUs while keeping the global batch size the same.

The project was built by the EarthDial authors at IBM Research and MBZUAI. If you're submitting this as your own entry, change the wording to say what you contributed, such as the demo, deck and video. Don't present the research itself as yours.
